1858.description: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was successfully laid, connecting Ireland to Canada. It ceased functioning after only three weeks.

1866.description: A permanent and more reliable transatlantic telegraph cable was successfully laid, drastically reducing communication times between Europe and North America from weeks to minutes.

1870.description: The first submarine telegraph cable link connecting Great Britain to India, Singapore, and Australia (via the Australian Overland Telegraph Line) was established.

1898.description: By the end of the 19th century, a sophisticated "web" of submarine telegraph cables linked Europe and North America, including the French Atlantic telegraph cable.

1902.description: The telegraph across the Pacific Ocean was completed, connecting the U.S. mainland to Hawaii. The trans-Pacific segment of the British "All Red Line" also connected Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

1903.description: The First Transpacific telegraph cable connected San Francisco, Honolulu, Midway, Guam, and Manila in the Philippines.

1921.description: The Key West–Havana submarine cables entered service. Executive Order No. 3513 was also issued in the United States, relating to applications for submarine cable licenses.

1951.description: Western Union integrated electronic amplifiers into their non-loaded cables at the edge of the continental shelf.

1956.description: The first transatlantic telephone cable, TAT-1, commenced service, connecting Scotland and Newfoundland. This coaxial cable system initially carried 36 telephone channels and marked the beginning of global telephone communications via submarine cables.

1959.description: TAT-2, the second transatlantic telephone cable, was laid from France to Newfoundland. This year also saw the "Transatlantic Cables Incident," where a Soviet vessel was boarded by the USS Roy O. Hale in response to cable breakages.

1960.description: The 1960s marked the dawn of the satellite communication age, with the launch of Telstar 1 in 1962, the first active communications satellite. For a time, satellites became the primary choice for transoceanic communication.

1963.description: The AT&T cableship CS Long Lines was launched and laid TAT-3, a single-line transatlantic cable capable of carrying 128 channels. The Commonwealth Pacific Cable System (COMPAC) also linked Canada, Hawaii, Fiji, New Zealand, and Australia.

1964.description: TPC-1, the first trans-Pacific coaxial telephone cable, entered service connecting Hawaii, Midway, Wake Island, Guam, and Ninomiya, Japan.

1965.description: TAT-4 entered service between New Jersey and France, expanding transatlantic voice and data capacity.

1970.description: Communications-grade optical fiber was developed at Corning. TAT-5, utilizing transistors, went into service between Rhode Island and Spain, carrying 845 channels.

1975.description: TPC-2 expanded trans-Pacific coaxial capacity across Guam, Okinawa, Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

1976.description: TAT-6 (SG), the highest-capacity analog coaxial transatlantic telephone cable carrying 4,000 voice circuits, entered service between Rhode Island and France.

1978.description: A significant commitment was made by AT&T, GPO, and Standard Telecommunications Laboratories for TAT-8, scheduled for a decade later, to be fiber-optic instead of coaxial.

1982.description: TAT-2 was retired as emerging fiber-optic submarine cable technology neared deployment.

1983.description: TAT-7, the final coaxial transatlantic telephone cable, entered service between New Jersey and England before the transition to optical fiber.

1984.description: The ANZCAN coaxial submarine cable system entered service, replacing COMPAC and linking Australia, Norfolk Island, New Zealand, Fiji, Hawaii, and Canada.

1986.description: The first commercial international fiber-optic submarine cable was laid across the English Channel between the United Kingdom and Belgium.

1987.description: A report on the erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) was released, a key breakthrough enabling long-haul all-optical submarine communication.

1988.description: TAT-8, the first trans-Atlantic fiber optic cable, entered service. This revolutionary cable had a capacity equivalent to 40,000 telephone circuits, a tenfold increase over its predecessor, marking a decisive shift from satellites back to submarine cables.

1989.description: TPC-3, the first trans-Pacific fiber-optic cable, and PTAT-1, the first privately financed trans-Atlantic fiber-optic cable, entered service.

1990.description: Commercial internet providers began connecting across transoceanic fiber-optic cables, marking the beginning of a new era for global communication.

1991.description: The World Wide Web launched publicly, driving exponential demand for intercontinental submarine bandwidth.

1992.description: TAT-9, TAT-10, and TPC-4 entered service, while the CS Long Lines cableship completed its historic career.

1993.description: TAT-11, SAT-2, APC, and PacRimEast entered service, extending fiber-optic connectivity across the Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Asia-Pacific.

1994.description: CANTAT-3 and Columbus-II entered service alongside the first deployments of optically amplified submarine cable systems.

1995.description: RJK (Russia-Japan-Korea) and PacRimWest entered service, expanding fiber-optic networks across the western Pacific.

1996.description: TPC-5CN and TAT-12/13 entered service, introducing self-healing SDH optical ring architectures with Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers (EDFAs) across the Pacific and Atlantic.

1997.description: FLAG Europe-Asia (FEA) and APCN (Asia Pacific Cable Network) were completed, connecting Europe, the Middle East, and Asia.

1998.description: Between 1998 and 2003, approximately 70% of new undersea fiber-optic cable was laid in the Pacific Ocean, reflecting the rapid global expansion of the internet.

1999.description: SEA-ME-WE 3—spanning 39,000 km and 39 landing points from Western Europe to East Asia and Australia—entered service alongside Columbus-III.

2000.description: China-US CN entered service as global internet usage soared to 361 million users, followed by a telecom boom and subsequent market consolidation.

2001.description: TAT-14, Japan-US CN, APCN-2, and AJC entered service during the peak of the early-2000s submarine cable construction wave.

2002.description: SAT-3/WASC, SAFE, and Tata TGN-Pacific entered service, while TAT-8 was retired after 14 years of operation.

2003.description: First-generation fiber-optic cables including TAT-10, TAT-11, TPC-3, and Gemini were retired as high-capacity DWDM systems took over.

2004.description: TAT-9 and PTAT-1 were decommissioned as next-generation transatlantic networks carried the majority of IP traffic.

2005.description: SeaMeWe-4 entered service, providing a high-capacity terabit corridor between Europe, the Middle East, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

2008.description: Major submarine cable disruptions in the Mediterranean Sea and Middle East highlighted the vulnerability of this critical infrastructure, causing widespread internet slowdowns and outages.

2015.description: Major technology companies like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft began directly investing in and building their own undersea cables.

2016.description: TeleGeography's Submarine Cable Map showed 321 undersea cable systems globally.

2018.description: TeleGeography's Submarine Cable Map showed 366 undersea cable systems.

2019.description: A "building boom" in undersea cables occurred, with approximately 378 submarine cables in service.

2020.description: The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant spike in internet traffic, with new system spending rebounding to $2.7 billion, while legacy systems TAT-14 and Columbus-III retired.

2021.description: Global internet bandwidth continued its upward trajectory, rising by 29%.

2022.description: Global internet bandwidth rose by 28%, reaching 997 terabits per second (Tbps). TeleGeography mapped 486 cable systems.

2023.description: Global internet bandwidth increased by 23%, reaching 1,217 Tbps, and the number of cable systems grew to 529.

2024.description: Major sections of 2Africa, IAX, IEX, and PEACE went live, while the historic 39,000 km SEA-ME-WE 3 cable retired after 25 years of service.

2025.description: The global internet user base is projected to reach 5.6 billion, with nearly 600 active and planned submarine cable systems worldwide.
